{{Short description|English mathematician (1907–1969)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Harold Douglas Ursell''' (16 April 1907 &ndash; 8 December 1969), known as '''H. D. Ursell''', was an English [[mathematician]] who is best known for the [[Ursell function]].

==Life==
Ursell was born in [[Warwickshire]] in 1907, the youngest of six children, and was raised in [[Birmingham]]. He was educated at [[Tile Cross Academy|Central Grammar School]] and [[King Edward's School, Birmingham|King Edward's School]] in the city, before studying mathematics at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], where he graduated as a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]] with distinction in Part II of the [[tripos]] in 1926 at the unusually young age of 19.<ref name="Young">{{citation|first=L. C. |last=Young|title=   Harold Douglas Ursell |journal=   Bull. London Math. Soc. |year=1970|volume= 2|pages= 344&ndash;346|doi=10.1112/blms/2.3.344|issue=3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Historical Register of the University of Cambridge Supplement, 1921-30 |date=1932 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |page= 120}}</ref> It was while still an undergraduate that he made his name with the Ursell function, laying the foundations of a cluster expansion theory through the study of imperfect gases. At Cambridge he was the beneficiary of numerous prizes, including the famed [[Smith's Prize]], and in 1929 was elected to a fellowship at Trinity after studying almost period functions under the tutelage of [[Abram Besicovitch|A. S. Besicovitch]]. He was also a Choate Fellow at [[Harvard University]] during the years 1930–31.<ref name="Young"/>

Greatly influenced by both Besicovitch and [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]], Ursell left Cambridge while still a young man, following W. P. Milne to take up a position at [[Leeds University]] in 1933.<ref name="Young"/> There he remained for almost the entirety of his career, rising to the position of Reader in 1948. During his time at Leeds he wrote a number of articles on a variety of topics, becoming noted for his ability to rebut existing theorems using counter-examples; he was, however, perhaps best known for his diligent supervision of undergraduates and postgraduates alike. In 1967, he accepted a professorship at [[Calgary University]] in Canada, but died suddenly of a stroke two years later.<ref name="Young"/>

Ursell was not related to the German-born fellow Trinity mathematician [[Fritz Ursell]], who taught at [[Manchester University]].
